content.problem_summary: Given two binary strings `a` and `b`, compute their sum and return it as a binary string.
core_idea: Simulate elementary school addition from the least significant bit, walking `a` and `b` from the end with two pointers and prepending each result bit to a growing string.
Track a `carry` variable across iterations to propagate overflow from one bit position to the next, exactly like manual binary addition.
invariant: At the start of each loop iteration, `carry` correctly represents the carry-out from all bit positions already processed (i.e., positions to the right of `a_ptr`/`b_ptr`).
`binary_sum` always holds the correctly computed suffix of the final answer for the bits already consumed.
trap: After the main loop ends, one of `a` or `b` may still have remaining higher-order bits that still need the carry applied — easy to forget and drop digits.
A leftover `carry == 1` after all digits are consumed must be prepended as an extra leading `'1'`.
Building the result by prepending (`binary_sum = bit + binary_sum`) is O(n) per operation in Python, making the whole solution O(n^2) instead of O(n).
recognition_clue: Two sequences of digits/characters that must be combined arithmetically from the least significant end with carry propagation → process from the back with two pointers and a carry variable.
Different-length strings representing numbers → main pairwise loop plus two separate cleanup loops (or a single loop using `0` as a default digit) to flush the longer string's remaining digits.
takeaway: Carry-based digit-by-digit simulation generalizes to any base (binary, decimal, hex) addition problem — the pattern is: pointers from the end, per-digit sum with carry, then flush leftover digits from the longer operand.
When building a string result by repeated prepending, prefer appending and reversing (or using a list + join) at the end to avoid the hidden O(n) cost of each prepend.
